result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.stoer_wagner()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a global minimum cut of an undirected graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L41972-L42049){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.stoer_wagner(capacity=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Stoer-Wagner minimum cut](/assets/graphs/stoer-wagner.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same weighted graph, with no source or sink. The cheapest split of the whole graph is not between the two triangles (capacity 3) but around G: its two light accent edges A–G and C–G cost 1 + 1 = 2.0. The card gives that value and the two sides, A to F (teal) and G alone (violet)." width="100%"} The global minimum cut is the cheapest way to split the graph into two non-empty parts, over all possible pairs of sides, without fixing a source or sink in advance. Its value is the graph's edge connectivity when every edge has capacity 1, and in general it measures how easily the network falls apart: a low value means some group of nodes hangs on by a few (or light) edges. The Stoer-Wagner algorithm finds it directly, without running a max-flow computation for every pair of nodes. Capacities are read as in `max_flow()`: from the edge attribute named by `capacity=`, else an attribute called `"capacity"`, else the edge weight on a weighted graph, else `1.0`. Parallel edges add up and self-loops are ignored. A disconnected graph has a minimum cut of `0`, between a component and the rest. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [capacity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute holding capacities (see above). If `None` (default), use the `"capacity"` attribute, the weight, or `1.0`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[float, tuple[list[int], list[int]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `(cut_value, (side_a, side_b))`, each side a sorted list of node IDs, with the side holding the smallest node ID first. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed, has fewer than two nodes, or has a negative capacity. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two triangles joined by one edge: the global minimum cut is that single bridge: ::: {#9d646899 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "D")]) ) value, (one, other) = graph.stoer_wagner() label = graph.get_label_from_id value, [label(n) for n in one], [label(n) for n in other] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (1.0, ['A', 'B', 'C'], ['D', 'E', 'F']) ``` ::: ::: With weights as capacities, a heavy bridge is no longer the weak point; a lightly tied node is: ::: {#5ac4f667 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} weighted = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B", 3.0), ("B", "C", 4.0), ("C", "A", 3.0), ("C", "D", 1.5)]) ) value, (one, other) = weighted.stoer_wagner() value, [weighted.get_label_from_id(n) for n in other] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (1.5, ['D']) ``` ::: :::
